payload.headline: Task Management covers scheduled and dependency-driven task automation with a Kanban board, calendar view, Excel bulk import and AI-assisted task planning; of 15 tickets marked ready for release, 7 are backed by code the analysis could read, 7 could not be confirmed from the code it saw, and 1 (holiday-calendar scheduling) appears not to be built.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a background scheduler that ticks every 30 seconds and runs several tasks at once on separate worker threads, task dependencies where a task waits for all its prerequisites, a drag-and-drop Kanban board with status lanes, a calendar view of scheduled runs, Excel/CSV/JSON bulk import with a downloadable template, and an AI planner that turns a plain-language description into a structured list of tasks.
payload.what_is_unclear: The underlying task record itself (statuses, types, priorities), the range of recurrence options (daily/weekly/monthly/cron), task chaining rules, task input/output modes and artifact storage, the task approval gate, notifications via Teams or email, and the create/edit task form could not be confirmed — the files examined were a keyword-selected slice and did not include the relevant code, so this is not evidence the features are absent. Separately, the holiday-calendar and working-days-only scheduling ticket looks wrong: the task scheduling form shown supports only a simple one-time schedule and notes that repeat/cron scheduling was removed, with no holiday or country fields present.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to the code behind the seven unconfirmed tickets (task record and statuses, recurrence options, chaining, input/output, approval, notifications, task editor form) and to confirm whether holiday-aware scheduling was deliberately dropped so that ticket can be corrected.
payload.caveat: Several supporting documents cited for these tickets were flagged as not describing this repository, and specific widgets they referenced were not found, so documentation alone should not be treated as evidence here.

payload.headline: The Co4E visual workflow builder — a node-graph editor with a wave-by-wave execution engine, run modes, run history and custom agent personas — is covered by 14 tickets all marked ready for release, and the code backs up 8 of them while the other 6 could not be confirmed from the code that was examined.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a working visual workflow canvas (drag-and-drop nodes, zoom, pan, connect and delete), an execution engine that runs nodes in dependency order and passes each step's output into the next, parallel fan-out to sub-agents, automatic self-verification rounds with a configurable limit, run modes for automatic, plan-only and manual step-by-step execution, run history with saved workflow snapshots, and user-defined custom agent personas for workflow steps.
payload.what_is_unclear: Six items could not be settled because the specific code was not among the files reviewed: the full list of node types (Join, IF/Switch, Start, End), conditional IF/Switch branching and the skipping of gated nodes, permission presets (inherit, read-only, standard, full), importing and exporting workflows between instances, and the newer request to add an attachment-folder and URL source to a workflow step. This reflects which files were looked at, not evidence that the features are absent.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where conditional branching, permission presets and workflow import/export live, and to confirm whether the attachment-folder and URL fields have been added to the step configuration screen — these can likely be resolved with a short walkthrough.
payload.caveat: Some supporting documentation referenced during the analysis appeared to describe a different product, so it was disregarded; the conclusions above rest on the code itself.

payload.headline: The desktop app's interface layer — theming, navigation, settings, dashboard charts, notifications and several dialogs — is largely present in the code, with 8 of 12 tickets backed by implementation and 4 that the review could not settle.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows working dark/light theming with accent colours, a collapsible navigation rail with sub-tabs, a settings dialog covering provider/theme/language choices, in-app toast notifications, a model-routing on/off toggle, a smooth dashboard metrics chart, a full file-editing dialog, and an end-to-end permission request/confirmation flow. Several of these are only partially visible — for example the toast's auto-hide timing and the permission dialog's own screens were not seen, though the surrounding wiring is.
payload.what_is_unclear: Four tickets could not be confirmed either way: the first-run welcome dialog with nickname/email setup, the workspace member-management dialog, a general "Update UI/UX" item, and a broad intent to improve the AI flows the core team actually uses. The last two carry no specific described behaviour to look for, and for the first two the files inspected simply did not touch those screens — this is not evidence they are missing.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to confirm the status of the file editing dialog, which is marked To Do but appears fully built, and to attach concrete deliverables to the two open-ended UI/UX tickets so progress on them can be tracked.

payload.headline: Cowork Chat covers the in-product chat experience — conversation panel, composer, agent tooling, code execution and file deliverables — and of its 11 tickets the code review confirmed 3 (the streaming chat panel with history, and saving/revising deliverable files into the workspace), while the remaining 8 could not be settled from the code that was examined.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a working chat loop that streams replies incrementally and keeps conversation history, plus an agent tool that writes finished deliverables (documents, spreadsheets, text and CSV files) into a workspace output folder, overwrites a file when the same name is re-saved, and can produce several files in one session.
payload.what_is_unclear: The user-interface side of the area — the composer with file/link/image attachments, the per-tab model picker and skill attachment control, the output file tree, the terminal panel, and stop/cancel handling — was not confirmed, because the interface files that would settle it were never opened during the review; likewise the sandboxed code runner and the Code agent's file read/write/edit tools, where only configuration and an intentionally empty rule document were seen. The in-progress "Superpowers" item has no description beyond its title, so there was nothing concrete to check it against.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point the next review at the Cowork tab's interface and code-execution code so the composer, model picker, output tree, terminal and cancel behaviour can be checked directly, and ask for a one-line description of what the in-progress "Superpowers" item is meant to deliver.
payload.caveat: Several of the documents consulted during the review were flagged as describing a different codebase, so any absences they mention should not be read as evidence about this product.

payload.headline: The security and sandboxing area covers isolating risky code execution, resource caps, network blocking, certificate trust, security policy rules and audit logging — of 11 tickets, 6 are backed by code we could read, 4 could not be settled from the code examined, and 1 describes something different from what the named component actually does.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows working process containment on Windows with CPU, memory and disk caps, a default-deny network posture for sandboxed work, a configurable security policy engine driven by an editable rulebase with per-layer toggles, per-host certificate trust with a CA-bundle override, and two separate audit trails recording tool calls, permission decisions, security blocks and every sandbox execution attempt.
payload.what_is_unclear: Four items could not be confirmed from the code examined — the Hyper-V based sandbox VM, prompt-injection fencing of untrusted content, role-based access control over workspaces and tasks, and the rulebase review task (a review leaves no code trace by design); this means unconfirmed, not missing. Two partially-confirmed items also have gaps: no log pruning or expiry logic was seen behind the audit retention policy, and the URL guard and macro-blocking parts of the network ticket were not visible.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to confirm three things directly: whether role-based access control and prompt-injection fencing exist elsewhere in the product, and whether audit log retention is actually enforced or just implied by the file layout. Separately, the certificate trust ticket is still marked In Progress although the feature looks complete — worth a status check.
payload.caveat: One ticket describes 'file integrity verification' but the component of that name does something else entirely: it enforces a Windows low-integrity execution level rather than verifying files. The ticket title and the code are talking about two different meanings of 'integrity', so the ticket may simply be misnamed rather than the work being wrong.

payload.headline: The Agent Platform — role-based chat agents, custom agent personas, admin and manager screens, an in-app help assistant, and agent security monitoring — is largely backed by code, with 8 of 10 tickets supported, 2 not settled, and 1 backlog item that appears already built.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a catalogue of agent personas with role-specific base prompts plus user-added instructions, admin and user-facing screens for creating, editing and deleting agents, a floating in-app help assistant, security checks that block risky agent actions and email an administrator when they fire, and a bundled library of reusable skills seeded at startup into an editable skill manager.
payload.what_is_unclear: Two items could not be confirmed from the code that was examined: a general tool registry classifying tools as read, write or execute (only one connector family showed a read/write split), and a human approval step for command execution (automated security blocking was found, but no approve-or-deny prompt or pending-request queue). Some supporting documentation referenced during the review described a different codebase, so it carried no weight.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team where the tool scope registry and the human command-approval step live, and confirm whether the skill-standardisation item still open in the tracker should be closed given the skill library already present.
payload.caveat: Several reference documents cited in the analysis describe a different repository and name files that do not exist here, so any conclusions resting on them should be discounted.

payload.headline: Monitoring & Admin covers a monitoring dashboard with security, activity and agent views plus a set of admin tabs (agents, tools, icons, sandbox, skills); all ten tickets are marked ready for release, and the code review backed up five of them while the other five could not be settled from the code that was examined.
payload.what_is_there: The product clearly has a Monitoring section built as its own navigation area with sub-pages, and the configuration behind it names specific views for security events, agent status, action logs and MCP call history, including which of them a sub-admin is allowed to see. There is also supporting evidence for admin tabs covering agents, tools and custom icon management.
payload.what_is_unclear: The analysis never saw the code for the Monitoring screens themselves, so the overview page of system health metrics, the MCP call history view, filtering on action logs, sandbox capacity management and the skill create/edit/delete tab could not be confirmed either way — the sandbox capacity settings that were found appear to sit under Settings rather than Monitoring. Even for the confirmed items, only the surrounding wiring and configuration were seen, not the screens themselves, so behaviour such as real-time alerting remains unchecked.
payload.suggested_action: Ask someone with access to the running build to walk through each Monitoring sub-tab and confirm the five unconfirmed ones — overview metrics, MCP call history, action log filtering, sandbox capacity management and the skill manager — actually appear and work as described.
payload.caveat: One of the reference documents used during the review describes a different product area and was disregarded; it should not be treated as evidence about this feature area.

payload.headline: The Knowledge & RAG area covers codebase structure graphs, interactive graph viewing in a browser, and persistent codebase memory — three of nine tickets are backed by code, while the six remaining tickets (mostly around retrieval quality, knowledge packaging and shared agent context) could not be confirmed from the code that was reviewed.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a working codebase structure graph that renders as an interactive, searchable diagram in the browser with an entity-type legend, plus a persistent codebase memory service with indexing, project listing, architecture overviews, call-path tracing and code snippet retrieval, wired into application settings. All three of these are marked 'Release it' in the tracker, which matches what the code shows.
payload.what_is_unclear: The analysis could not settle the six remaining tickets: knowledge-graph extraction from file content, semantic similarity search, a portable knowledge pack specification, standardising how agents collect context from RAG/Search/MCP, upgrading knowledge into a packaged form with sources and citations, and numeric measurement of semantic search quality including Japanese. The files reviewed were selected by keyword and covered unrelated concerns, and the one piece of documentation that described a knowledge search capability was flagged as belonging to a different build — so this is an absence of evidence, not evidence of absence.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where semantic/similarity search and retrieval scoring actually live, so those six tickets can be re-checked against the right part of the codebase.
payload.caveat: One documentation source repeatedly surfaced describing project-knowledge search, but it was judged not to describe this repository and the functions it referenced were not found — worth confirming which build that document belongs to.

payload.headline: The LLM provider and model-routing area covers eight items all marked ready to release; the code clearly backs four of them (multi-provider setup, the Claude integration, model health probing, and context-window management), while four others — the OpenAI-compatible provider, model auto-routing, and model pricing/budget alerts — could not be confirmed from the code that was examined.
payload.what_is_there: The product supports picking between five model providers, has a working Anthropic/Claude integration with live streaming responses and retry handling, probes candidate models for latency and quality before use, and automatically compresses long conversations so they stay within a model's context window. There are also configuration samples describing intended routing behaviour such as cost-based policies and per-provider concurrency limits.
payload.what_is_unclear: The analysis did not see the code behind the OpenAI-compatible provider (chat, streaming, model listing, custom endpoints), the automatic model routing and queueing logic, or the per-model pricing, currency conversion and budget alerts. That is an absence of evidence in the slice of code reviewed, not proof the features are missing — a routing package and pricing file exist by name but their contents weren't read.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the owning engineer to point to where OpenAI-compatible provider calls, model auto-routing, and pricing/budget alerting are implemented, and confirm each has been exercised end to end before these are treated as shipped.
payload.caveat: Some of the supporting evidence for the pricing and budget item came from material flagged as not describing this codebase, so treat that item as genuinely open.

payload.headline: This area covers connecting the product to external tools — user-configured connector plumbing for CAD/CAE and Microsoft 365, plus the underlying tool-connection client — and the code confirms the connector framework and its management settings, while five of the eight items could not be settled from the code reviewed.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a working, user-configurable connector system with categories for CAD, CAE, Microsoft 365 and other tools, ready-made presets, two connection modes (launching a local tool process or calling a REST service), secret masking, a connection test, and migration of older configuration into the new model — all built to sit behind a Settings panel for managing connectors, which is present in the repository. Generic plumbing for CAD/CAE tools such as CATIA, NX and ANSYS exists, though no vendor-specific integration was seen, which fits the item still being in progress.
payload.what_is_unclear: The analysis could not confirm the HTTP connection option for tool servers (only the local-process option was visible), the built-in Microsoft 365 server and its local file read/write/list tools, the reusable tool-contract deliverable (schema, sample manifests, validation tests and a single tool registry), or the item about building a real project capability on top of the existing tooling. In each case the relevant files were either not included in the subset of code examined or the supporting documents turned out to describe a different codebase, so nothing was proven missing.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the owning engineer to point to where the HTTP transport, the Microsoft 365 server and its local file tools, and the tool-contract documents and schema live, so those five items can be checked directly rather than inferred.
payload.caveat: Several reference documents cited for these tickets were found to describe a different repository, so any expectations set by those documents should be re-confirmed with the team.

payload.headline: The Workspace area covers seven features marked ready for release; the code review found supporting implementation for three of them (project management, the knowledge-graph visualisation, and chat history sessions) and could not confirm the other four either way.
payload.what_is_there: There is a workspace home for managing projects, an interactive knowledge-graph view with colour-coded entity types, legend and node search, and a full chat-history store behind the sidebar that lists, renames, deletes, pins and searches past conversations. Chat session creation and tracking are also present.
payload.what_is_unclear: Multi-tab chat panels with independent sessions, the folder picker for choosing AI-edit target files, member management with role-based permissions, and workspace trash with restore were not settled — the files examined simply did not cover them, which is not evidence they are missing. The similarity-search side of the knowledge graph and the rename/delete/duplicate project actions were also not directly visible, though the surrounding features were.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where access control, workspace trash, the AI-edit folder picker and multi-tab chat sessions are implemented, so those four can be confirmed before the release sign-off.
payload.caveat: Some of the reference documentation consulted during the analysis was flagged as describing a different codebase, so it contributed nothing either way for the access control and trash tickets.

payload.headline: Platform Integrations covers seven connector and execution features marked as released, of which four (Jira issue tracking, Java runtime support, link previews, and the workflow/flows engine) are backed by code the analysis could read, while three (Git operations, batch processing, and Windows COM) could not be confirmed from the code that was examined.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a working read-only Jira connector (search and issue lookup with authentication, plus Jira link resolution in previews), a Java runtime locator used to run an external PDF tool, a URL preview feature that fetches pages, caps size and substitutes explanatory notes when a page can't be read, and a workflow layer that defines and saves multi-step flows seeded at application start.
payload.what_is_unclear: Git workspace operations, application batch processing and Windows COM integration were not settled — the files pulled in matched on words like 'workspace' and 'batch' rather than the actual features, so there is no evidence either way. For the workflow engine, flow definition and storage are visible but the part that actually runs a flow was only referred to indirectly; similarly, Java support is shown as locating a Java runtime for one specific tool rather than general code execution.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where Git operations, batch processing and Windows COM live so those three can be checked directly, and confirm whether 'Java code execution' and 'Flows execution' mean more than what is currently visible.
payload.caveat: The Windows COM ticket is still open in the tracker, so its unconfirmed status may simply reflect work not yet done rather than a gap in the analysis.

payload.headline: The Dashboard & Analytics area covers usage charts, cost reporting and AI-driven usage insights; all six tickets are marked ready for release and the code backs up four of them, with two not confirmed either way.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows a dashboard with a usage-trend chart at week/month/year granularity, an AI feature that summarises token-usage habits including busiest day and hour, an AI cost-saving recommendation with a one-click apply control, and a display-currency picker that saves the chosen currency and converts cost figures.
payload.what_is_unclear: The token usage and cost overview with its today/week/month/all period filter, and the stat cards for total/input/output/cache tokens and cost per bucket, could not be confirmed because the main dashboard screen file was never examined directly — similar token cards were found in the monitoring screen instead. Several of the confirmed items were matched from names and surrounding wiring rather than the full implementation, so depth of behaviour is not established.

payload.headline: AI Edit covers AI-assisted document editing — presentation editing, document text/style extraction, an Office document viewer and image generation — and four of its six tickets are backed by code we could read, with Excel editing and AI-generated file previews not settled either way.
payload.what_is_there: The code shows in-place editing of PowerPoint decks (text, position, size, fonts and image replacement), extraction of text, styles and structure from documents, conversion of Office and OpenDocument files into a previewable form for an in-app viewer, and text-to-image generation against a DALL-E-style image service including model selection for the edit picker.
payload.what_is_unclear: Two tickets could not be confirmed: AI-driven Excel cell editing (only read-only spreadsheet extraction and an account template import/export were seen) and the AI-generated file preview feature (the relevant screen exists but its code was not among the files examined). Some supporting documentation appears to describe a different product, so it was not treated as evidence.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where AI-driven Excel cell editing and the AI preview generation live, so those two tickets can be checked against the right code.
payload.caveat: Documentation cited alongside these tickets appears to describe a different system, so it was disregarded when assessing the Excel and preview claims.

payload.headline: The DevOps and utilities area covers six supporting capabilities marked ready for release — file-path and cloud-folder detection, log retention, run timing, an in-app console view, dependency checking and sandbox preparation — of which only the path utility could be matched to code in this review.
payload.what_is_there: The code confirms a working utility that detects a user's OneDrive location from the environment (with sensible fallbacks) and resolves configuration file paths. A sandbox runtime and its policy settings also exist, though not the setup scripts the sandbox ticket describes.
payload.what_is_unclear: Log rotation and cleanup, execution timing, the in-app console with a hide option, runtime dependency verification and sandbox preparation scripts could not be confirmed — in each case the files reviewed were about something else (per-run output cleanup, task ordering, planning notes) or no files were retrieved at all. This is a limitation of what the review looked at, not evidence the features are absent.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the developer to point to where log retention, run timing, the console display, dependency checks and sandbox preparation live, so those five can be confirmed directly.

payload.headline: Core Platform covers the desktop application shell, configuration, shared application state and multi-language support; of the five tickets here, only the language-switching work was matched to code, while the other four could not be confirmed from what the analysis read.
payload.what_is_there: The analysis found working evidence of in-app language selection: a language picker in the top bar, a translation function, and a saved language preference that takes effect immediately without restarting. Everything else in this area — the desktop window shell with navigation and system tray, the JSON settings file with upgrade-on-load and environment overrides, and the shared application state with connection caching — was not matched to code that was examined.
payload.what_is_unclear: The analysis only looked at a keyword-selected slice of the codebase, so the four unconfirmed tickets are unsettled rather than shown to be missing; it did pick up a partial signal that the shared-state provider setup exists. For the language feature, the exact three locales claimed (English, Vietnamese, Japanese) were not visible, and the final ticket is a strategy task about merging fork changes upstream, which code cannot answer either way.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the owning engineer to point to where the application shell, settings file handling and shared state live so those three tickets can be checked directly, and confirm the upstreaming ticket separately as a process item rather than through code.

payload.headline: QA and testing covers five items — an automated test suite, a QA report with test cases and bugs, security hardening tests, workflow-feature tests, and UI/UX testing — and the code review was unable to confirm or rule out any of them.
payload.what_is_there: The tickets describe automated tests across the product (workflow engine, routing, transfers, security features) plus manual QA activity such as executed test cases, documented bugs, and UI/UX testing. What the review actually saw was production code — configuration, connectors, history, and the workflow user interface — with no test files or QA artefacts among it.
payload.what_is_unclear: Whether any of these tests or QA records exist is unconfirmed: the files examined were a keyword-selected subset that happened to contain no tests, and a supporting document referenced by the tickets was explicitly about a different codebase. This is an absence of evidence, not evidence that the testing work is missing.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point directly at where the tests and QA outputs live — the test folder, the test run results, and the bug list — so the area can be checked against the real artefacts rather than inferred from application code.
payload.caveat: One referenced supporting document does not describe this repository, so any ticket detail drawn from it should be re-checked with the team.

payload.headline: This area covers five proposed new capabilities — production bug handling, new-ticket handling, an expanded project graph screen, a business-overview screen, and a configurable report-output screen — and the code reviewed did not confirm any of them.
payload.what_is_there: The only thing the reviewed code clearly shows is an existing application shell with dashboard, schedule, workspace, cowork and structure sections, including a project structure graph already embedded inside the workspace area. None of the five proposed new screens or workflows could be matched to working code.
payload.what_is_unclear: All five tickets are unconfirmed: two are written as broad placeholders with no concrete requirement to check against, and for the others the files examined did not include the relevant screens, so the analysis could neither confirm nor rule them out. Some supporting documents referenced during the review appear to describe a different project, so they carry no weight here.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to the specific screens or workflows for each of these five items so they can be re-checked, and tighten the two placeholder tickets into concrete requirements before the next review.
payload.caveat: Several documents cited as evidence were flagged as not describing this codebase, so they should not be treated as support for any of these tickets.

payload.headline: Notifications covers four capabilities — a Microsoft Teams webhook, Outlook email sending, an in-app notification centre, and event-driven routing — and the code confirms the two outbound channels while the other two could not be confirmed from what was examined.
payload.what_is_there: There is a working Teams integration that posts formatted notification cards to a Teams webhook, including a plain-text fallback and error handling, and a separate path that sends email through a locally installed Outlook, including a check for whether Outlook is available. Both of these are direct send paths for individual messages.
payload.what_is_unclear: The analysis found nothing about an in-app notification bell with unread counts, and nothing resembling a central dispatcher or routing layer that decides which events go to which channel — only two standalone senders. Because only a keyword-selected slice of the code was read, this does not mean those pieces are absent, just unconfirmed. It is also unconfirmed whether the Outlook email path is wired into scheduling or task editing.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where the in-app notification centre and the event routing layer live, so those two tickets can be checked directly; separately, confirm whether the Outlook email work marked 'In Progress' is in fact finished, since the send path itself appears complete.

payload.headline: The Skills area covers a set of ready-made skills shipped with the product plus the ability for users to manage and attach their own; the code confirms the built-in skill library, while the management screen and the skill picker could not be confirmed from the code reviewed.
payload.what_is_there: There is a working mechanism that ships a packaged set of built-in skills and seeds them into the user's skill collection, keeping track of which ones have already been installed so they can be refreshed. One of the five named built-in skills is directly visible, and its numbering suggests the others sit alongside it.
payload.what_is_unclear: The analysis could not confirm the skill management features — creating, editing and deleting user-defined skills — or the picker used to attach a skill to a task or chat. Both are referenced indirectly by the bookkeeping the built-in library relies on, but the code examined was a keyword-selected slice and did not include them.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where skill creation/editing and the skill picker live so those two tickets can be checked directly, and confirm all five built-in skills are present in the shipped library.
payload.caveat: Some supporting documentation reviewed during the analysis was flagged as describing a different repository, so it carried no weight here.

payload.headline: Usage and telemetry covers recording what the product does per model turn and rolling that up into shared usage summaries; the shared aggregation half is backed by code we could read, while the per-turn usage tracker itself was not confirmed.
payload.what_is_there: There is working code that collects usage and audit records written as line-by-line log files, gathers them across multiple machines, and exposes them for summarising usage and audit activity. A usage tracker component and a token-estimation capability are referenced and appear to exist.
payload.what_is_unclear: The actual contents of the usage tracker were never examined, so the specific claims about logging an event per model turn, caching those events to file, and offering a summarise interface could not be checked either way. The analysis only saw a keyword-selected slice of the code, so this is unconfirmed rather than missing.
payload.suggested_action: Ask whoever owns the usage tracker to walk through per-turn event logging and the summarise call once, so that ticket can be closed out with confidence.

payload.headline: This area covers sending notifications and accepting remote commands through team chat tools (Microsoft Teams and Slack), and the code we examined did not confirm either piece of work.
payload.what_is_there: The code we saw does include a background task scheduler that pops up a desktop/tray notification when a task finishes, plus admin email alerts elsewhere. What we could not find was anything for posting notifications into a team's chat channels, any configurable schedule for those notification checks, or any way to control the product remotely from a chat tool.
payload.what_is_unclear: Neither ticket could be settled: the Teams notification settings did not appear in the files reviewed, and for the Slack remote integration no relevant code was retrieved at all and the ticket itself is barely more than a title. Because the review only looked at a keyword-selected slice of the repository, this is not evidence the work is absent.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the developer on these two tickets to point to where the Teams notification settings and Slack remote integration live, and get the Slack ticket written up with actual requirements beyond its title.
payload.caveat: Some of the architecture documentation pulled in during the review appeared to describe a different system, so background material for this area should be treated with care.

payload.headline: The Performance area contains a single ticket described only as a performance update, and the code review could not link it to any specific change in the product.
payload.what_is_there: The ticket carries no description of what was to be made faster, only a title and role information. The code that was examined covers the visual workflow canvas and workflow tab, including connection routing and tracking of individual flow runs, but nothing there could be tied to the ticket's intent.
payload.what_is_unclear: Whether any performance work was done at all is unclear, because the ticket does not state a measurable or checkable change to look for. Supporting design documents reviewed alongside the code were found to describe a different codebase, so they added nothing.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the ticket's author to record what was slow, what was changed, and how the improvement was measured, so the work can be confirmed.

payload.headline: Backend Refactoring covers a single in-progress housekeeping ticket to restructure backend code, and the analysis could not confirm from the code whether any of that restructuring has happened.
payload.what_is_there: The only related material found is a written refactoring plan describing an intended new structure for the backend, alongside unrelated internal policy documents. The components the plan refers to were not found in the code that was examined.
payload.what_is_unclear: Because the ticket names no specific deliverable, there is nothing concrete to check the code against, so whether refactoring work has started, stalled, or is being done elsewhere in the codebase remains unsettled.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the owner to restate the ticket as one or two observable outcomes (which parts of the backend, and what should look different when done) so progress can be tracked.

payload.headline: Documentation covers a single in-progress task to produce business and detailed design documents from the existing source code, and the code review could not confirm its state either way.
payload.what_is_there: The only item in this area is a deliverable to write business design and detailed design documentation derived from the current system. What the analysis found nearby related to agent security and sandboxing rules rather than design documentation.
payload.what_is_unclear: Whether any of the design documentation has actually been drafted could not be established, largely because a documentation deliverable leaves no code trace and one document that surfaced was explicitly noted as belonging to a different system.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the ticket owner to point to where the business and detailed design documents live, or to share a current draft, so progress can be tracked outside the codebase.

payload.headline: This area covers a single planning task: reviewing the existing building blocks of the Cowork Local product and deciding which parts to reuse, improve or build from scratch — the code review could neither confirm nor rule out that this review has been done.
payload.what_is_there: The underlying pieces the review is meant to assess do exist in the product: request routing between language models, connections to external tools and services, and the agent that runs Cowork's workflows.
payload.what_is_unclear: The deliverable here is a written assessment rather than working software, so there is nothing in the code that could show whether the evaluation happened. The task's 'To Do' status was not challenged by anything seen.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the owner whether the assessment write-up exists yet, and if so, store it somewhere linked to the ticket so its completion is visible outside the tracker.

payload.headline: The requirement-review flagship product — reviewing requirements against project knowledge and supporting evidence — is still marked To Do in the tracker, and the analysis could not find code confirming it either way.
payload.what_is_there: The code that came up in the search was an admin-managed catalogue of agent presets (search, monitoring, collaboration, knowledge graph, scheduling, security and help types). Nothing in it relates to reviewing requirements or assessing evidence drawn from project knowledge.
payload.what_is_unclear: Whether any requirement-review capability exists elsewhere in the product is unresolved: the analysis only saw a keyword-selected slice of the codebase, and one supporting document it found was explicitly not about this codebase, so it proves nothing here.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team which part of the product is meant to deliver requirement review, so that specific area can be looked at directly rather than by keyword search.

payload.headline: Quality and safety assessment — the plan to replace subjective judgement with evidence-backed PASS/WARN/FAIL grades and map internal controls to the CASAN H1–H7 framework — is the only item in this area, and the code reviewed did not confirm it either way.
payload.what_is_there: The code that was examined includes security policy rules that block or deny certain actions, and a separate mechanism that scores and routes work to models based on fit. Neither of these is the structured PASS/WARN/FAIL grading with supporting evidence, nor the CASAN control mapping, that the ticket describes.
payload.what_is_unclear: Whether any of the intended grading and control-mapping work exists elsewhere in the product could not be established, because only a keyword-selected slice of the codebase was read. The ticket is also still open in the tracker, so its absence here is consistent with not having started.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the owning engineer whether any evidence-based quality grading or CASAN control mapping exists yet, and if not, confirm the ticket is genuinely unstarted rather than partly built somewhere unexamined.

payload.headline: The work-breakdown-structure area covers creating and running team tasks from a plan, Excel import/export, AI-generated task breakdowns, and Kanban, calendar and graph status views; the code examined did not settle how much of this exists.
payload.what_is_there: The files reviewed show closely related building blocks: an Excel template with import and export for account data, date-grid logic that could underpin a calendar view of scheduled tasks, and a holiday lookup. None of it directly demonstrates the task creation and execution flow, the AI-generated breakdown, the Kanban or graph views, or task dependencies.
payload.what_is_unclear: Whether the ticket's features are built is unconfirmed — the analysis only saw a keyword-selected slice of the repository, and one referenced task-related file was never shown. One supporting document appears to describe a different system, so it was not relied on.
payload.suggested_action: Ask the team to point to where task creation, the AI breakdown, and the Kanban/calendar/graph views live, and re-run the check against those areas.
payload.caveat: One document cited as evidence appears not to describe this codebase, so it carries no weight here.
